input.strategy_title: Audit logging for model inference traffic
input.strategy_markdown:
## Problem Statement

Financial-services customers cannot pass compliance reviews because inference
traffic on RHOAI leaves no audit trail: there is no record of who invoked which
model endpoint, when, and with what outcome. Auditors require tamper-evident,
structured audit events for every inference request. Without this, two
strategic renewals are at risk this fiscal year.

## High-Level Requirements

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| HLR-1 | P0 | Every inference request through a KServe endpoint emits an audit event capturing caller identity, model/version, timestamp, and response status (not payloads). |
| HLR-2 | P0 | Audit events are delivered to the cluster audit sink with at-least-once semantics and are not lost on component restart. |
| HLR-3 | P1 | Administrators can enable/disable inference auditing per project from the Dashboard. |
| HLR-4 | P2 | A common audit event schema is defined and published so future components (pipelines, workbenches) emit compatible events. Note: the schema in this item is the format HLR-1's events must conform to — HLR-1 cannot ship before the schema is settled. |
| HLR-5 | P2 | Documentation covers enabling auditing and interpreting events. |

## Affected Components

- KServe
- Dashboard

## Out of Scope

- Auditing of non-inference traffic (pipeline runs, notebook activity) — future
  strategies will adopt the HLR-4 schema
- Long-term audit storage and retention tooling (customer-provided)

## Open Questions

None — the audit sink interface is the standard cluster logging forwarder.

# Define and publish the common inference audit event schema

## Description

This epic delivers the common audit event schema that all inference audit events must
conform to: a defined, versioned event format capturing caller identity,
model/version, timestamp, and response status (explicitly not request/response
payloads), published so that future components (pipelines, workbenches) can emit
compatible events. It is the prerequisite for the inference audit event emission
work — that work cannot ship before this schema is settled.

## Scope

- Define the common audit event schema for model inference traffic, covering at
  minimum: caller identity, model and version, timestamp, and response status.
- Explicitly exclude request and response payloads from the schema.
- Define the schema so it is extensible to future emitting components (pipeline runs,
  notebook activity) without breaking compatibility for existing consumers.
- Publish the schema in the appropriate midstream location so downstream
  implementations and future strategies can reference it.
- Settle schema decisions needed by the emission work: event structure, required
  versus optional fields, and versioning approach.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A schema document exists that defines the audit event structure with fields for
  caller identity, model/version, timestamp, and response status.
- The schema documents that payloads are out of scope and defines no payload field.
- The schema is published and referenceable by name/version by consuming
  implementations and by future components (pipelines, workbenches).
- The emission work for inference traffic can be implemented against the published
  schema without further schema-blocking decisions outstanding.
- Extensibility for future emitting components is addressed (a compatibility or
  versioning story is documented).

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-4 (P2; elevated to P0 by priority inheritance — it gates P0 HLR-1): common
  audit event schema defined and published so future components emit compatible
  events.

# Emit audit events for KServe inference traffic with reliable delivery to the cluster audit sink

## Description

This epic delivers audit event emission for every inference request through a KServe
endpoint, plus reliable delivery of those events to the cluster audit sink (the
standard cluster logging forwarder). It also delivers the serving-side enforcement of
per-project auditing enablement that the Dashboard administrator toggle drives. This
is the core compliance capability of the strategy: a tamper-evident, structured
record of who invoked which model endpoint, when, and with what outcome.

## Scope

- Emit one audit event per inference request through a KServe InferenceService
  endpoint, conforming to the published common audit event schema: caller identity,
  model/version, timestamp, and response status.
- Do not capture or emit request or response payloads.
- Deliver emitted events to the cluster audit sink (standard cluster logging
  forwarder) with at-least-once semantics.
- Ensure events are not lost on component restart (durable buffering or equivalent
  mechanism between event generation and sink delivery — design choice for the
  implementing team).
- Implement per-project enablement enforcement: when auditing is disabled for a
  project, inference traffic in that project does not emit audit events; when
  enabled, it does. Expose the per-project enablement configuration surface that the
  Dashboard administrator toggle writes.
- Cover both KServe deployment modes where applicable (serverless and raw deployment).
- Tamper-evidence is provided at the cluster audit sink (the standard cluster logging
  forwarder and the customer's audit infrastructure that consumes it), not by the
  emission code: this epic's responsibility is to deliver complete, structured audit
  events to that sink; long-term retention and tamper-proof storage are customer
  provided and out of scope per the strategy.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given auditing is enabled for a project, when an inference request is served
  through a KServe endpoint, then an audit event conforming to the published common
  schema (caller identity, model/version, timestamp, response status) is emitted —
  measured by inspecting events received at the cluster audit sink.
- Given any inference request, no request or response payload content appears in the
  emitted audit event.
- Given auditing is enabled for a project, when the emitting component restarts, then
  in-flight/generated events are still delivered (no loss) — measured by event counts
  at the sink across a restart window.
- Delivery to the cluster audit sink exhibits at-least-once semantics (duplicates
  permitted, loss not permitted).
- Given auditing is disabled for a project, inference requests in that project
  produce no audit events; given it is re-enabled, subsequent requests produce
  events — measured at the sink.
- Audit event emission does not break inference request serving (existing
  InferenceService behavior and status conditions remain functional).

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): every inference request through a KServe endpoint emits an audit event
  capturing caller identity, model/version, timestamp, and response status (not
  payloads).
- HLR-2 (P0): audit events delivered to the cluster audit sink with at-least-once
  semantics, not lost on component restart.
- HLR-3 (P1, serving-side enforcement half): per-project enable/disable enforcement
  and the configuration surface the Dashboard toggle drives.

# Per-project inference auditing toggle in the Dashboard

## Description

This epic delivers the administrator-facing control for inference auditing in the
Dashboard: administrators can enable and disable inference auditing per project. It
is the user-facing half of per-project auditing — the Dashboard writes the
per-project enablement configuration that the serving-side audit emission enforces.

## Scope

- Add an administrator control in the Dashboard to enable/disable inference auditing
  for a project.
- Surface the current per-project auditing state (enabled/disabled) in the
  Dashboard.
- Write the per-project enablement through the configuration surface exposed by the
  serving-side auditing capability (the Dashboard acts on Kubernetes CRs; it owns no
  data plane).
- Respect OpenShift authentication and project-scoped RBAC: only administrators (not
  regular project users) can change the auditing setting.
- Follow existing Dashboard patterns for per-component settings and feature flags.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an administrator is viewing a project, when they enable inference auditing
  for that project, then the setting persists and the serving side emits audit
  events for subsequent inference requests in that project — measured by events
  observed at the cluster audit sink.
- Given an administrator disables inference auditing for a project, then subsequent
  inference requests in that project produce no audit events.
- The Dashboard reflects the current per-project auditing state on load.
- A non-administrative project user cannot change the auditing setting — measured by
  RBAC behavior on the controlling configuration.
- The control is available for projects using KServe model serving, in both serverless
  and raw deployment modes where the Dashboard distinguishes them.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P1, administrator UI half): administrators can enable/disable inference
  auditing per project from the Dashboard.

# Document enabling inference auditing and interpreting audit events

## Description

This epic delivers customer-facing documentation for inference audit logging:
how to enable auditing (including the per-project Dashboard control), and how to
interpret the audit events received at the cluster audit sink. Documentation runs
through the Red Hat docs content process and is written against what was actually
built.

## Scope

- A documentation topic covering how to enable inference auditing, including the
  administrator per-project toggle in the Dashboard.
- A documentation topic covering how to interpret inference audit events at the
  cluster audit sink: field meanings per the published common audit event schema
  (caller identity, model/version, timestamp, response status), and the explicit
  statement that payloads are not captured.
- Coverage of operational notes implied by the delivery semantics: at-least-once
  delivery (duplicates are possible) and behavior across component restarts.
- Cross-references to the compliance motivation (audit trail for inference traffic)
  where the docs set supports it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Published documentation explains how to enable and disable inference auditing per
  project from the Dashboard, accurate to the shipped administrator control.
- Published documentation explains the structure and meaning of inference audit
  events, accurate to the published common audit event schema.
- Documentation is technically reviewed against the implemented behavior (serving
  side and Dashboard) before publication — reviewed by someone who verified the
  steps against a running system.
- Documentation states that request/response payloads are not captured.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-5 (P2): documentation covers enabling auditing and interpreting events.

  the strategy frames it as the format for inference audit events.

## Criterion Details

### 1. HLR Coverage (2/2)
All five HLRs map to epics and the traceability matrix is present and accurate: HLR-1/HLR-2 (P0) → E002; HLR-3 (P1) → E002 (enforcement) + E003 (admin UI); HLR-4 (P2) → E001; HLR-5 (P2) → E004. No P0 HLR is missing. Priority inheritance is correct: E001 is elevated to P0 because HLR-4 gates P0 HLR-1 by the strategy's own note, and E001 sits first on the critical path. E004's P0 priority is the sanctioned docs-authoring exception (strategy priority Critical → P0) and correctly does not push priority upstream. The HLR-3 enforcement bundling into the P0 epic is not priority collapse: per the decomposition rules, a lower-priority HLR is bundled when it is a config override falling out of the same implementation surface (the per-project gate lives in the emission code path), while the genuinely deferrable piece with its own surface — the Dashboard UI — is a separate P1 epic (E003). Splitting enforcement out would force the emission and gating halves of one code path into sequential epics with no independent user value for the backend half alone.

### 2. DAG Coherence (2/2)
Diagram and frontmatter are fully consistent: E001 deps [], E002 deps [E001], E003 deps [E002], E004 deps [E001, E002, E003] — exactly the five diagram edges, drawn dependency → dependent per convention. No cycles, no invalid edges. Each edge is justified: E001→E002 is a Rule 13 build-against artifact edge (the published schema is the format the emission code builds against; the strategy explicitly states HLR-1 cannot ship before the schema is settled — this is a genuine artifact dependency, not a configuration reference). E002→E003 is justified: the Dashboard builds against the per-project enablement configuration surface (CR) that E002 defines; the alternative ordering would force two epics to define the same data structure independently, which the boundary rules forbid. The three edges into E004 are Rule 11 docs-authoring-last edges (valid, not serialization flags).
